In August 1854, the Soho neighbourhood of London was overwhelmed by a cholera epidemic so swift and lethal that over 500 residents died within ten days. The General Board of Health attributed this, as they attributed all such outbreaks, to "bad air" — the miasma theory, which held that disease spread through atmospheric corruption rising from filth and decay.
A local physician had been sceptical for years. He had written a pamphlet challenging miasma theory but lacked evidence to make the medical world listen. This time, he went methodically door to door, interviewing survivors and the families of the dead, asking one steady question: where did you get your water? He plotted every fatality as a small black bar on a large-scale street map of the area, aligning each bar with the address of the deceased.
The resulting image was stark — a dense bloom of marks surrounding a single public water pump on Broad Street, thinning sharply with distance from it. He presented his map to the local Board of Guardians and persuaded them to remove the handle from the pump. His map is now considered one of the founding documents of modern public health and an early masterwork of a discipline that would not receive its name for another century.
What discipline — the study of disease patterns, causes, and effects in populations, often using geographic distribution — did this physician's work help establish? And what broader category of cartography does his map represent?
